name: Big Dipper
label: Homestead
lede: Two guitarists from the wreckage of Kansas and Boston bands, a flying-saucer sleeve, and one major-label album that made them miserable.

eras.title: Two bands fall apart, one porch fills up
eras.text: The Embarrassment end in Kansas, Volcano Suns lose two members in Boston, and the leftovers meet through a mutual friend named music. By spring 1986 they have demos and a record deal but no name.

years.src: The College Crowd Digs Me · Wikipedia
years.h: [[The Embarrassment|487904ff-d3ef-477e-813a-c27548bc0570]] quit; Bill Goffrier moves to Boston for art school
years.p: The Wichita band that mailed its own tapes to the world stopped playing when two members relocated to Boston. Goffrier, the guitarist, enrolled in graduate art studies there.
years.xp:
The Embarrassment formed in Wichita, Kansas in 1979 and built a following by basement recording, tapes mailed to labels, college radio and constant touring. Goffrier says they opened for Iggy Pop, Public Image Ltd. and Pete Shelley, and never landed a major deal.

He told an interviewer he wasn't looking to start another band in Boston. That changed at a Volcano Suns show.

years.src: Wikipedia · Rock Town Hall · The College Crowd Digs Me
years.h: Gary Waleik and Steve Michener walk out of [[Volcano Suns|4837e8d3-a13f-4670-9684-82970411f4bc]]
years.p: Sixteen months in, and before the band's first album came out, the guitarist and the bassist left drummer [[Peter Prescott|f69ea4d3-4065-49ff-b076-585bfc6e79ff]]'s new band.
years.xp:
Prescott, late of [[Mission of Burma|db9d25d7-a85b-4a29-b2ff-8f5b69ed691e]], formed Volcano Suns in spring 1984. Wikipedia says he had auditioned for a drummer's spot in another band and took two of its members instead. Waleik has described the Suns as artistically promising but volatile.

Goffrier caught a Volcano Suns show in mid-1985 and got talking to Waleik, an Embarrassment fan. Their songwriting sessions, on a porch, became Big Dipper.

years.h: Bill Goffrier and Gary Waleik: two songwriters, one porch
years.p: Goffrier told an interviewer it wasn't a band at first, just three people trading songs, the two guitarists plus bassist Steve Michener.

years.h: A demo tape gets an unrequested contract from Homestead
years.p: Waleik says the band sent demos to Homestead's Gerard Cosloy in May 1986 and got a deal offer back before they had picked a name.
years.xp:
Drummer Jeff Oliphant, Waleik's cousin, had played speed metal in XS. The six-song demo included "Faith Healer," which got regular college radio play.

Waleik calls the group an experimental pop band, drawing on the Soft Boys, the odder Beatles and the artsy end of punk and power pop.

eras.title: Homestead: sleeves painted with UFOs
eras.text: Two years, one EP, two albums, all on Homestead. Goffrier's flying saucers wrap the cover of Heavens and a Swiss farmer's Pleiades story turns up on Craps.

years.src: The College Crowd Digs Me · Music Museum of New England
years.h: First gig: opening for the Mekons at The Rat
years.p: Goffrier remembers the debut show as a support slot for the Mekons at Boston's Rat.
years.xp: The Rat, on Kenmore Square, was Boston's basement rock room. Big Dipper became a Boston regular after this, and the Music Museum of New England lists the Rathskeller and the Channel among their local haunts.

years.h: Boo-Boo EP and the "All Going Out Together" 12-inch
years.p: The debut EP arrives on Homestead in 1987, with a UK release through Demon Records.

years.h: Heavens: produced by Paul Q. Kolderie, sleeve by Goffrier
years.p: A UFO painting by Goffrier fronts the debut album. AllMusic calls it one of the finest American indie albums of its era.
years.xp:
Paul Q. Kolderie produced. Waleik says Heavens was the peak of the first run: they spent months writing and rehearsing, and "couldn't wait to record that album."

The song "Mr. Woods" was covered by Gigolo Aunts on a 1996 benefit compilation. NME gave the record 5 out of 10 at the time.

years.p: "Semjase" is about Billy Meier, the Swiss farmer who claimed contact with beings from the Pleiades. The band called the record a pop album.
years.xp:
The Boston Globe praised its "winsome, off-center melodies" and hooks. It closes the Homestead contract; Rock and Roll Globe describes Craps as the end of a three-album deal.

"Ron Klaus Wrecked His House" outlived everything else here: in 2016 it was used in the film Gold, and it appears on the soundtrack.

q: We signed too early. We were ahead of our time.
years.h: Big Dipper signs to Epic, before the alternative gold rush
years.p: Their management pushed for it, the band says, on the argument they had done all they could on a small label.
years.xp: Epic signed four indie-leaning bands at once: Big Dipper, O Positive, Social Distortion and the Rave-Ups. Once Social Distortion took off, Michener says, the label lost interest in the rest.

years.src: Rock and Roll Globe · Wikipedia · The Agit Reader · The New York Times
years.h: Slam: horns, samples and a click track
years.p: Recorded in North Carolina with Steve Haigler, the Epic debut has 14 songs and closes on a cover of Mott the Hoople's "All the Way from Memphis."
years.xp:
Michener says they split the sessions into four phases by style, taking a cue from Beatles recording histories, and played to a click track for the first time. The New York Times ran a feature titled "Big Dipper Combines Punk With Melody" in April 1990.

The Boston Globe found the band in fine form; The Village Voice gave it a C+. Waleik says a few songs are wonderful but the record is not a good one.

years.h: The Slam cover the band hated
years.p: Epic hired professionals, spent real money, then showed the band a sleeve they disliked. Told it was too late to change, Goffrier calls it the major-label experience in a nutshell.
years.xp:
Michener is harsher, calling the cover "basically unforgivable" and his least favorite thing about the record.

Because Epic (Sony) owns the master, the band cannot reissue Slam without Sony's permission.

years.src: Rock and Roll Globe · The Agit Reader
years.h: Steve Michener and Gary Waleik agree over lunch that he should go
years.p: The summer Slam tour was ending, around a July show at New York's Marquee, when the bassist worked out his exit with Waleik at a restaurant called Nosmo King.
years.xp: Goffrier says the label "really didn't care at all about us" and that it was discouraging. Tom Brewitt took over on bass, according to The Agit Reader.

years.h: Epic drops the band; "Approach of a Human Being" 7-inch appears on Feel Good All Over
years.p: Wikipedia and the Music Museum of New England both say Epic let them go within about a year of Slam.
Waleik says he carried on for two years after Michener left, then walked away.
years.xp: The band had been working with session players and left unreleased material, which resurfaced on the third disc of the 2008 anthology.

eras.title: Supercluster and the second act
eras.text: A Merge box set gets the band back onstage. Twenty-two years after Slam there is a new album, on a label that wanted them.

years.p: Boo-Boo, Heavens and Craps, remastered, plus 15 unreleased songs from after Slam. Tom Scharpling of The Best Show wrote the introduction.
years.xp: Pitchfork gave the anthology 7.8 out of 10. Waleik credits Scharpling's persistent campaigning, from 2004, for the reunion.

years.p: Wikipedia dates the reunion performances to April 2008, the month after the box set.

years.h: Three songs land in Rock Band
years.p: "All Going Out Together," "She's Fetching" and "Younger Bums" became downloadable tracks in the game.

q: Almost Ready was the only label we could find that had any confidence in us.
years.src: The Agit Reader · Beats Per Minute · The Rumpus
years.h: Crashes on the Platinum Planet: first new album in 22 years
years.p: Released by Almost Ready Records, the only label they could find with confidence in them, Waleik says.
years.xp:
Waleik says that over four years the band had convened only sporadically to record. He produces NPR's Only a Game and Goffrier teaches art in Boston; Michener is a nurse in Oregon and Oliphant works in finance.

Robert Pollard of Guided by Voices, an early fan, once told Waleik he thought Big Dipper were the 20th best rock band ever, Waleik says.
